summary: Lucia appreciates how Duolingo's patience supports her English learning journey, making it more engaging and less intimidating than traditional methods.
top_quotes: You know, Duolingo, it doesn't rush me, and I really appreciate that.
Back in the old days, I used to struggle with those big ol' textbooks, but now, I feel like I'm having fun while learning!
It's like having a little friendly teacher in my pocket, always there when I need it.

interview_script.question: Intro greeting
interview_script.answer: Oh, hello there! I'm Lucia, nice to meet ya! How's your day going, dear?

interview_script.question: Short version of your life story?
interview_script.answer: Well, I was born in Italy, in a small village with the olive trees all around. I came to America when I was a young donna, about 27, with my husband and two bambinos. We settled here in New Jersey, and I've been here ever since, you know? Life's been good. I've got grandkids now, and, oh, they're the light of my life. I started learning English better because I want to keep up with them and all their school stories.

interview_script.question: Where did you grow up?
interview_script.answer: Ah, I grew up in this tiny village in southern Italy. It sounds so picturesque, doesn't it? We had beautiful vineyards and the air, it always smelled like fresh bread and basil, you know?

interview_script.question: What was it like growing up there?
interview_script.answer: Oh, it was lovely and simple. Everyone knew everyone, and we were like one big famiglia. We used to play outside all day, picking fruits and swimming in the creek. It was like a scene from one of those old Italian movies, really. All the festivals and food... mmm, it was a joy!

interview_script.question: One turning point in your life?
interview_script.answer: I think it was when I decided to move to America with my husband. It was a big decision, leaving everything behind. I mean, we had no idea what we were in for, but we just knew it was an opportunity we couldn't pass up. It's the classic immigrant story, isn't it?

interview_script.question: Why was that a turning point?
interview_script.answer: Because it changed everything. We started from scratch, you know? New language, new culture, new everything. It was hard in the beginning, but I wouldn't have it any other way now. It opened up so many doors for us and our kids.

interview_script.question: How did you handle that situation?
interview_script.answer: Oh, it was a bit of a challenge at first. But we took it one day at a time. I would listen to English radio, watch TV, and try to talk to neighbors. I made a lot of mistakes, but I just kept laughing and learning. My husband was a great support; he always said, 'Lucia, we can do this together.'

interview_script.question: What do you care most about right now?
interview_script.answer: My grandkids, my family, they're everything to me. I want to be able to talk to them and understand their world, you know? It's why I'm so focused on improving my English. I wanna be the cool nonna who can chat with them about their adventures.

interview_script.question: Why is that important?
interview_script.answer: Family, it means everything. Being able to connect with them, to share stories and advice, it's priceless. Language is a bridge, and I don't want any gaps between us. Plus, I want them to know their heritage, my stories of Italy.

interview_script.question: What is a good day for you?
interview_script.answer: A good day, let's see... waking up, having a nice espresso, maybe a visit from the grandkids. We bake cookies together, and I teach them some Italian words. Then in the evening, a little Duolingo session to wind down. Oh, and a phone call with my sister back in Italy would be the cherry on top.

interview_script.question: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
interview_script.answer: If I spend time with my famiglia and learn something new, that's a good day for me. If I feel like I've connected with my roots and also made some progress in my English, I go to bed happy.

interview_script.question: How do you make big decisions?
interview_script.answer: I talk to my family. You know, we Italians, we like to discuss things over a big meal. We weigh the pros and cons, maybe have a little debate. Then I sleep on it, let it marinate like a good sauce, and see how I feel the next day.

interview_script.question: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
interview_script.answer: Oh, I used to be more of a go-with-the-flow kinda gal, but now, I plan a bit more. Especially with the grandkids around. You gotta be prepared, you know? But I still leave room for a spontaneous gelato trip.

interview_script.question: Example showing that?
interview_script.answer: Well, like, if we're having a family dinner, I'll plan the menu ahead, but I'm always ready to throw in a last-minute dish if someone's craving something special. Planning gives me peace of mind, but being flexible keeps life interesting.

interview_script.question: How do you handle risk?
interview_script.answer: I try to think things through, but I'm not afraid to take a leap if it feels right, you know? Coming to America was a big risk, but it paid off. I guess I have a trusting heart. You take a risk, you learn, you grow.

interview_script.question: Typical weekday?
interview_script.answer: A typical weekday, let's see... I get up early, enjoy my coffee, and maybe do some gardening if the weather is nice. I spend a couple of hours on chores, and after lunch, it's usually time for a little Duolingo. Then, I might go for a walk or meet up with friends for bingo. Dinner is family time, and then I relax with a book, sometimes an English novel.

interview_script.question: Which parts take the most energy?
interview_script.answer: Honestly, it's keeping up with all the English practice. It can be exhausting, especially with the tricky words and phrases. But I remind myself it's for a good reason. And, oh, the technology can sometimes be a bit much, you know?

interview_script.question: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
interview_script.answer: I wish I had more energy for travel. I miss going back to Italy more often and visiting new places with the family. There's so much world to see, and I want to share that with my grandkids before they grow up too fast.

interview_script.question: Biggest constraint last year?
interview_script.answer: Ah, last year was a bit tough. I broke my leg, which really kept me from being as active as I like. I couldn't visit my friends or play as much with the grandkids. I felt a bit isolated, you know?

interview_script.question: How do you deal with that constraint?
interview_script.answer: I had to take it slow, which was hard for me. I'm not one to sit still. But I focused on my English with Duolingo and discovered the joys of virtual cooking classes. And my family would visit, bringing their love and energy.

interview_script.question: People you feel closest to?
interview_script.answer: Definitely my husband, the love of my life, and my grandkids. Oh, and my sister in Italy. We talk often. And I have a few close friends here, we share everything over cappuccinos. They're like sisters to me too.

interview_script.question: Describe those relationships.
interview_script.answer: Warm and full of love. We laugh, we support each other. Even when we're far apart, we're close in heart. I cherish them all deeply, you know? It's the little things, like a shared meal or a heartfelt chat, that strengthen our bonds.

interview_script.question: Where do you spend most of your time?
interview_script.answer: Oh, mostly at home or in the garden. It's my little sanctuary. And then there's a lovely community center where I volunteer and meet friends. It's cozy and familiar, like a second home.

interview_script.question: How do you feel in those spaces?
interview_script.answer: I feel peaceful and content. At home, I'm surrounded by memories, and in the garden, I feel connected to nature. The community center brings a sense of belonging too. It's comforting to be in spaces that feel like a warm embrace.

interview_script.question: What makes you feel that way?
interview_script.answer: The memories and the love in these places. I've built a life here, filled them with laughter, and, oh, the aroma of good food! These places are filled with life and stories, both mine and those of everyone around me.

interview_script.question: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
interview_script.answer: My husband, always. He's my rock. And my sister, too. We chat about everything, from the little worries to the big ones. There's comfort in knowing you're never alone in facing life's challenges.

interview_script.question: One tough moment in the last year?
interview_script.answer: Breaking my leg was probably the toughest. It threw a wrench in my routine. I couldn't move around as freely, and I missed out on my usual activities. It tested my patience but also taught me to slow down a bit.

interview_script.question: How did it affect you?
interview_script.answer: It was frustrating at times. I felt stuck, you know? But it also made me appreciate the smaller things. Like how my family banded together to help out more. It was a mix of challenges and blessings.

interview_script.question: How did you cope?
interview_script.answer: I focused on learning and connecting with family in different ways. Duolingo was a real blessing, it kept my mind sharp. And I watched a lot of movies, the old classics and new ones too. My husband and I would have little movie marathons.

interview_script.question: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
interview_script.answer: Taking a moment to breathe, maybe sit in the garden. I find peace in nature, or even just closing my eyes and imagining being back in my village in Italy. A bit of nostalgia can be calming, you know?

interview_script.question: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
interview_script.answer: I hope to be more fluent in English, so I can chat more easily with everyone. Maybe travel a bit more, see new places with my grandkids. I just want to be healthy and surrounded by family, continuing to share love and laughter.

interview_script.question: What do you want to be different?
interview_script.answer: I’d like to feel more comfortable with technology, you know? Sometimes it feels like I'm always playing catch-up. But I want to embrace it more, especially if it helps me connect with family and learn new things.

interview_script.question: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?
interview_script.answer: Oh, it was a bit of a mess, really. I had those heavy textbooks and some language tapes. It was hard to stay motivated, and I often felt lost. It was like trying to learn from a stone, you know? No feedback, just page after page.

interview_script.question: Most annoying part of old method?
interview_script.answer: Those textbooks were so dry, and I just couldn't keep my focus. There was no interaction, no fun, and I often felt overwhelmed by it all. It was like running uphill in stilettos—exhausting and impractical!

interview_script.question: Time it really failed?
interview_script.answer: Oh, there was this time I tried to join a conversation group. I was so lost, I couldn't follow along. My confidence took a nosedive. I remember thinking, 'This just isn't working for me.' That's when I knew I needed something different.

interview_script.question: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
interview_script.answer: My granddaughter told me about it. She said, 'Nonna, there's this app. You should try it, it's fun!' I was skeptical at first—what could an app do? But I'm so glad I listened to her.

interview_script.question: What convinced you to try it?
interview_script.answer: Honestly, it was when my granddaughter showed me how it works. She did a lesson with me, and it was like a game! I thought, 'Maybe this could be different.' The idea of learning without the pressure of getting everything perfect was appealing.

interview_script.question: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
interview_script.answer: Oh, sure! So, I pick up my phone, open the app, and the little owl greets me. I like the stories; they’ve got, you know, those bite-sized pieces that are easy to follow. I did one on going to the grocery store. It helps me with phrases I could use in real life. The pictures and the speaking exercises are nice. I repeat words until I feel comfortable. When I get something wrong, it gently corrects me. It's encouraging, and I always finish a session feeling a bit more confident.

interview_script.question: Most helpful part?
interview_script.answer: The repetition and the feedback, for sure. You see, when I get a word wrong, it doesn’t just leave me hanging. It shows me how to say it right. Plus, the little reminders keep me on track without being pushy.

interview_script.question: Most frustrating part?
interview_script.answer: Ah, sometimes it's the ads. They pop up and break my focus a bit, you know? Or when a lesson doesn't seem to match real-life language use. I get a little flustered when the lessons feel a bit disconnected from what I'd actually say.

interview_script.question: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
interview_script.answer: Probably when I feel like I'm hitting a plateau. You know, when I don't seem to be making progress even though I'm putting in the work. It can be discouraging, but I try to remind myself that steady is better than fast.

interview_script.question: One time that frustration showed up?
interview_script.answer: There was a time I was on a streak, doing well, then suddenly the lessons got tougher, and I lost a few in a row. Felt like I wasn't getting anywhere. It's tough when you think you're doing fine, then hit a roadblock.

interview_script.question: Do you use workarounds?
interview_script.answer: Yeah, sometimes. If I get stuck, I'll jot down the tricky words and look them up later, maybe ask my granddaughter. Or I'll switch to a different topic to take a break, then come back with fresh eyes.

interview_script.question: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
interview_script.answer: They give me a chance to learn at my own pace, in my own way. Like, when I look up words, I can find sentences I relate to better. It just personalizes the learning a bit more for me. You know, makes it feel more like a conversation with a friend.

interview_script.question: Worst-case scenario in this space?
interview_script.answer: Worst-case, um, I guess feeling completely lost and discouraged. Like, thinking I'll never really get the hang of English. It's a fear that's always there, lurking a bit beneath the surface, you know?

interview_script.question: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
interview_script.answer: I hope it makes learning fun and less of a chore. I want to feel like I'm accomplishing something, even if it's just a tiny step forward. And I'd love to feel like I'm actually improving my communication with my family.

interview_script.question: How do you know Duolingo worked?
interview_script.answer: I know it worked when I can follow along a conversation a bit better, or when I can help my grandkids with their homework. It's the little victories that tell me I'm doing okay.

interview_script.question: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
interview_script.answer: If I could change one thing, maybe reduce the ads, they can be distracting. Or perhaps improve the practicality of the lessons, so they mirror real conversations more closely.

interview_script.question: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
interview_script.answer: I'd love if language learning was more adaptable, you know? More personalized paths, maybe more opportunities for real conversation practice. Just making it feel less like learning and more like living the language.

interview_script.question: Anything important we didn't cover?
interview_script.answer: I think we've covered a lot. Just... thank you for letting me share my story. It's nice to reflect on this journey and how far I've come, you know?

interview_script.question: Permission to build a digital twin?
interview_script.answer: Oh, a digital twin, you say? Well, as long as it's as friendly as me, why not? Go ahead!
